query: For additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy with an fcc matrix, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs degradation during elevated-temperature exposure to oxidizing or reducing gases and why catastrophic failure may occur? Specify a controlled change that would reveal the governing behavior, predicted observations relative to the starting-state baseline, applicable exposure boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: In the additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 alloy with an FCC matrix, the degradation during elevated‐temperature exposure is controlled by a transition in oxidation behavior. At moderate oxygen partial pressures, diffusion leads to a continuous, protective Al/Ti-rich oxide scale that retards oxidation and preserves mechanical integrity. However, exceeding a threshold oxygen activity causes rapid, localized grain-boundary oxidation, which induces intergranular embrittlement and eventually catastrophic failure. Under reducing atmospheres, the lack of a stabilizing oxide scale results in internal oxidation and phase decomposition that also accelerates failure.
generation.material_initial_state: As-built, additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 with a fine FCC matrix, residual stresses, and characteristic AM microstructural features.
generation.intervention: Systematically vary the oxygen partial pressure (or the ratio of oxidizing to reducing gas species) while maintaining a constant high temperature (e.g., 700–800°C).
generation.conditions: Exposure to controlled atmospheres ranging from moderate oxidizing to strongly oxidizing (and compared with reducing conditions) at temperatures between 700–800°C.
generation.structural_mediator: The evolution and continuity of the surface oxide scale, particularly its behavior along grain boundaries.
generation.mechanism: At moderate oxygen levels, diffusion of Al and Ti forms a continuous, protective oxide scale that retards further oxidation. When oxygen partial pressure increases beyond a critical threshold, rapid oxidation at grain boundaries predominates, leading to localized embrittlement. Under reducing gas conditions, insufficient protective oxide development permits internal oxidation and possible phase decomposition, both promoting microcrack initiation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Under moderate oxygen partial pressures, a uniform, continuous oxide scale will develop and delay degradation, whereas higher oxygen partial pressures will induce discontinuous, grain-boundary oxidation accompanied by significant reductions in mechanical strength and earlier onset of catastrophic failure. In reducing atmospheres, internal oxidation and phase changes will correlate with premature degradation relative to the as‐built baseline.
generation.baseline: The as-built microstructure in inert or low-oxygen atmospheres, where minimal oxidation-induced degradation is observed.
generation.boundary: Temperature maintained between 700–800°C, with gas compositions specifically adjusted to vary oxygen partial pressures from moderately oxidizing conditions to strongly oxidizing (and compared with reducing conditions).
generation.uncertainty: The precise oxygen partial pressure threshold for transitioning from protective scale formation to severe grain-boundary oxidation and the exact kinetics of internal oxidation under reducing conditions remain to be quantitatively determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare multiple samples of the AM Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 alloy and expose them at 700–800°C under atmospheres with systematically varied oxygen partial pressures (and a set of reducing environments). Monitor the oxide scale evolution and grain boundary characteristics using in situ high-resolution electron microscopy and ex situ surface analysis (e.g., SEM/EDS). Simultaneously perform mechanical tests (e.g., tensile or creep tests) to assess the onset of degradation and failure.
measurements: Oxide scale morphology and composition via SEM/EDS
Mechanical strength and time-to-failure data from tensile/creep tests
Comparison of degradation behavior across varying oxygen partial pressures
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If, upon varying the oxygen partial pressure, there is no observable transition in oxidation mode (i.e., no switch from continuous protective scale to localized grain-boundary oxidation) or corresponding drastic mechanical property degradation (such as a sudden reduction in strength or earlier failure), then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Abstract This article presents the high temperature tensile and creep behaviors of a novel high entropy alloy (HEA). The microstructure of this HEA resembles that of advanced superalloys with a high entropy FCC matrix and L1 2 ordered precipitates, so it is also named as “high entropy superalloy (HESA)”. The tensile yield strengths of HESA surpass those of the reported HEAs from room temperature to elevated temperatures; furthermore, its creep resistance at 982 °C can be compared to those of some Ni-based superalloys. Analysis on experimental results indicate that HESA could be strengthened by the low stacking-fault energy of the matrix, high anti-phase boundary energy of the strengthening precipitate, and thermally stable microstructure. Positive misfit between FCC matrix and precipitate has yielded parallel raft microstructure during creep at 982 °C, and the creep curves of HESA were dominated by tertiary creep behavior. To the best of authors’ knowledge, this article is the first to present the elevated temperature tensile creep study on full scale specimens of a high entropy alloy, and the potential of HESA for high temperature structural application is discussed.

Abstract Oxidation behavior of a refractory AlNbTiVZr 0.25 high-entropy alloy at 600–900 °C was investigated. At 600–700 °C, two-stage oxidation kinetics was found: Nearly parabolic oxidation (n = 0.46–0.48) at the first stage, transitioned to breakaway oxidation (n = 0.75–0.72) at the second stage. At 800 °C, the oxidation kinetics was nearly linear (n = 0.92) throughout the entire duration of testing. At 900 °C, the specimen disintegrated after 50 h of testing. The specific mass gains were estimated to be 7.2, 38.1, and 107.5, and 225.5 mg/cm 2 at 600, 700, and 800 °C for 100 h, and 900 °C for 50 h, respectively. Phase compositions and morphology of the oxide scales were analyzed using X-ray diffraction (XRD) and scanning electron microscopy (SEM). It was shown that the surface layer at 600 °C consisted of the V 2 O 5 , VO 2 , TiO 2 , Nb 2 O 5 , and TiNb 2 O 7 oxides. Meanwhile, the scale at 900 °C comprised of complex TiNb 2 O 7 , AlNbO 4 , and Nb 2 Zr 6 O 17 oxides. The oxidation mechanisms operating at different temperatures were discussed and a comparison of oxidation characteristics with the other alloys was conducted. frame.system: An additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy exhibiting an fcc matrix microstructure, with the inherent as-built microstructural features (such as residual stresses, porosity, and fine grain structure) typical of AM processing.
frame.goal: To develop and test a mechanistic hypothesis that explains how degradation develops during elevated-temperature exposure to oxidizing or reducing gas environments and why catastrophic failure may occur, by linking microstructural evolution (e.g., scale formation, grain-boundary oxidation, or phase instability) to mechanical breakdown.
frame.limitation: The current lack of a definitive, testable mechanistic model that correlates the observed degradation (and subsequent catastrophic failure) with the interactions between the alloy’s microstructure and the prevailing chemical environment at high temperature.
constraints: A controlled change in a key parameter (e.g., gas composition or oxygen partial pressure) is required to reveal the governing degradation mechanism
The hypothesis must predict distinct observations relative to the starting-state baseline
Applicable exposure boundaries (temperature range and gas composition limits) need definition
Supporting evidence from prior related studies should be used
A clear falsification criterion must be established, where absence of predicted changes invalidates the hypothesis
frame.regime: Elevated-temperature conditions (e.g., >600°C) in controlled atmospheres that are either oxidizing (with a specified oxygen or water vapor level) or reducing (with, for instance, H2 or CO) to simulate service environments.
prior_attempts: Prior research on high-entropy alloys and conventional alloys has observed scale formation and internal oxidation phenomena but lacked a detailed in-situ correlation between gas environment chemistry and microstructural degradation leading to failure.

Previous studies have documented that AM alloys exhibit unique oxidation behaviors due to residual stresses and microstructural defects, yet these studies did not systematically vary the gas composition to isolate the key degradation mechanism.
frame.understanding: The working hypothesis is that the degradation—and subsequent catastrophic failure—of the AM high-entropy alloy is governed by a competition between the formation of a protective, continuous oxide scale (controlled by diffusion through grain boundaries and the alloy’s compositional segregation) and the development of localized oxide-induced embrittlement at critical microstructural sites. Under oxidizing conditions, selective oxidation (of, e.g., Al and Ti) may initially form a transient protective layer, but once a threshold oxygen activity is exceeded, rapid grain-boundary oxidation occurs, leading to intergranular decohesion. In reducing atmospheres, the absence of a stabilizing oxide may allow for sub-scale internal oxidation and phase decomposition that accelerates microcrack development. A controlled increase or decrease in the oxygen partial pressure (or alternately, the ratio of oxidizing to reducing gas components) should change the kinetics of scale formation versus internal oxidation, thus modulating the onset of catastrophic failure. If the predicted transition in oxidation mechanisms (e.g., a shift from protective scale growth to grain-boundary embrittlement) is observed within the defined exposure boundaries, it would support the hypothesis; failure to observe these trends would falsify it.

decision.trend: Earlier research on HEAs has moved from establishing processing–microstructure–property relationships to observing the effects of high‐temperature exposure on oxidation and degradation. For example, PMC7515071 investigated elevated-temperature wear in an Al-containing HEA, where oxide formation (e.g., spinel phase) was implicated in improving wear resistance, suggesting that oxidation kinetics are sensitive to the external environment. Separately, PMC7229066 studied additively manufactured CoCrFeMnNi alloys and reported microstructural features and precipitate formation at elevated temperatures, although without systematic variation of the gas atmosphere. These studies indicate that while oxidation or scale formation is recognized as affecting high-temperature performance, neither work directly isolated the role of gas composition (i.e. oxygen partial pressure) in controlling the competition between forming protective scales versus deleterious grain-boundary or internal oxidation. Thus, the trend has been to observe high-temperature phenomena in complex microstructures, with the need now to control the ambient chemistry to reveal mechanistic transitions.
decision.unsolved: A definitive, testable mechanistic model is still missing that correlates the controlled gas environment—specifically the oxygen (or oxidizing/reducing gas) partial pressure—with the microstructural evolution (continuous protective scale versus localized grain-boundary oxidation or internal oxidation) that ultimately governs catastrophic failure. The unsolved aspect is to determine how a controlled change (for example, tuning oxygen activity) can move the system from beneficial protective scale formation to rapid embrittlement and crack propagation.
decision.lever: Systematically vary the oxygen partial pressure (or oxidizing/reducing gas ratio) at a fixed high temperature (e.g., 700–800°C) while monitoring the evolution of oxide scale morphology and grain-boundary oxidation using in situ and ex situ high-resolution electron microscopy and surface analysis techniques.
decision.why: This controlled-variable approach directly follows the trend observed in earlier studies—where oxidation behavior impacts mechanical performance—but has not yet been isolated as the key parameter. By varying oxygen activity, the experiment can reveal the transition threshold at which a protective, continuous oxide scale gives way to rapid, detrimental grain-boundary oxidation or internal oxidation. The predicted observations (continuous scale and delayed failure under moderate oxygen activity versus rapid intergranular degradation and catastrophic failure above a threshold) and a clear falsification criterion (i.e., failure to observe any gas-pressure–induced transition in oxidation mode relative to the as-built baseline) will provide the requisite mechanistic correlate needed to address the open question.
